newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel business leaders slam high interest rates.
newsitem.headline: Israel business leaders slam high interest rates.

text.p: Israeli business leaders, bemoaning an overvalued shekel, high interest rates and a depressed capital market, pointed accusing fingers at the Bank of Israel on Tuesday at a symposium sponsored by the Treasury.

Dan Gilai, joint managing director of the brokerage house Sigma, said the rise in real interest rates to four percent from nil over the last four years was the main cause for the prolonged stock market slump.

"Only a reduction in interest rates in a gradual and organised fashion will bring the stock market back to the balanced situation it enjoyed in 1992," Gilai said. But he added: "The situation isn't going to change in the short run."
He called Bank of Israel policy inconsistent and reactive. "The Bank of Israel responds sometimes with hysteria" to economic developments, he said.

The Bank of Israel has adopted a restrictive monetary policy in a bid to contain inflation, expected to rise this year to 11 percent from 8.1 percent last year. The central bank has said it cannot cut interest rates significantly until the government reduces its budget deficit.

Gilai said foreigners still expressed interest in investing in Tel Aviv shares, especially since the 30-month-old market slump has left many stocks undervalued. But, he said, poor liquidity discouraged them.

Gideon Lahav, chairman of Israel Discount Bank, noted the role high interest rates played in buoying the shekel. He said the dollar was now 10 percent lower in real terms against the shekel than it was in 1993.
The shekel has been strengthened by capital imports, which have been encouraged by the widening interest rate differential between Israel and abroad.

Lahav estimated that the gap had widened to 11.5 percent today from eight percent in May 1995, when the central bank began raising short-term rates. The domestic base rate today is 15.2 percent, after reaching as high as 17 percent in July.
The strong shekel, he said, had caused the growth rate of Israel's industrial exports to fall to an estimated four percent this year from 17 percent in 1993.

Uzi Vardy-Zer, managing director of Housing & Construction Holding Co, blamed at least part of the current slowdown in residential construction on Bank of Israel directives limiting construction lending by banks. The central bank has expressed concerned about the banks' exposure to the property sector.
He said the rise in housing prices had slowed since 1994, but added that the sector was not heading into a deep slump.
David Arzi, chairman of electronics concern Nice Systems, warned that Israel's high-tech sector had difficulty operating in the current exchange rate environment.
He said he was less concerned with the shekel's strength than with his inability to predict costs because the exchange rate does not consistently reflect Israel's inflation.
Companies like Nice sell almost entirely overseas, earning their income in dollars while their costs are in shekels.
Arzi warned that if conditions did not improve, high-tech companies would have to transfer operations overseas. "Don't send us to Ireland or to Silicon Valley," he said.
